definitions.definition: The study of how physical laws and spiritual truths are connected.
definitions.example: Like using math to describe how gravity works, but also how God's grace works.

definitions.definition: The idea that one equation can produce both good and bad outcomes depending on the situation.
definitions.example: A knife can be used to cut food or to hurt someone—same tool, different result.

definitions.definition: Something that completely destroys or cancels out something else.
definitions.example: When you add a positive number and its negative, they annihilate to zero.

definitions.definition: The limits or settings that control how a system behaves.
definitions.example: The temperature setting on an oven is a parameter that controls how hot it gets.

definitions.definition: A number that represents how much a being can choose freely, not just follow rules.
definitions.example: A rock has W=0 because it can't choose to fall; a person has W>0 because they can decide.
definitions.first_appearance: Foundation > The Architecture > W — The Free Will Variable

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure how much information can be sent through a channel.
definitions.example: Like figuring out how many text messages you can send without errors over a noisy phone line.
definitions.first_appearance: Foundation > The Architecture > Shannon Measurement Layer

definitions.definition: Endpoints or states that a system naturally moves toward over time.
definitions.example: A ball rolling down a hill will eventually stop at the bottom—that's the attractor.

definitions.definition: Moves back and forth between two points or states.
definitions.example: A pendulum swinging back and forth oscillates.

definitions.definition: In a way that is completely predictable, with no randomness or choice.
definitions.example: A clock ticks deterministically—you know exactly when the next tick will happen.

definitions.definition: How much importance or consequence an action has in terms of right and wrong.
definitions.example: Stealing a candy bar has less moral weight than stealing a car.

definitions.definition: Giving up something valuable for a greater purpose or for someone else.
definitions.example: A parent working extra hours to pay for their child's education is a sacrifice.

definitions.definition: The force that pulls objects with mass toward each other.
definitions.example: The reason an apple falls from a tree and the moon orbits Earth.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > The 10 Laws > Law 1 — Newton-Einstein

definitions.definition: The shortest or most natural path between two points in curved space.
definitions.example: An airplane flying a curved route over the Earth to save fuel follows a geodesic.

definitions.definition: Using force or threats to make someone do something.
definitions.example: A bully using threats to take your lunch money is coercion.

definitions.definition: The size a mass must be squeezed into to become a black hole.
definitions.example: If you compressed Earth to the size of a marble, it would have a Schwarzschild radius.

definitions.definition: A point where gravity becomes infinite and the normal laws of physics break down.
definitions.example: The center of a black hole is a singularity.

definitions.definition: The boundary around a black hole where nothing, not even light, can escape.
definitions.example: Once you cross the event horizon, you can never come back out.

definitions.definition: The exact point where a small change causes a big, often sudden, effect.
definitions.example: Boiling water at 100°C is a critical threshold—it turns from liquid to gas.

definitions.definition: The maximum rate at which information can be sent without errors over a noisy channel.
definitions.example: The fastest speed you can download a file without getting corrupted data.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 1 > Shannon Channel Capacity

definitions.definition: A measure of how clear a signal is compared to background noise.
definitions.example: A good radio station has a high signal-to-noise ratio; static means low ratio.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 1 > Shannon Channel Capacity

definitions.definition: When God shows or makes known something that was hidden.
definitions.example: A sudden understanding of a truth you didn't see before.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 1 > Shannon Channel Capacity

definitions.definition: The idea that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, linked by E=mc².
definitions.example: A tiny amount of mass can be converted into a huge amount of energy, like in a nuclear bomb.

definitions.definition: Something that changes energy from one form to another.
definitions.example: A power transformer changes high voltage to low voltage for your home.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or substance that something is made of or built on.
definitions.example: Concrete is the substrate for a road; the road is built on top of it.

definitions.definition: A fixed number that tells you how to change one unit of measurement into another.
definitions.example: The number 2.54 is the conversion constant between inches and centimeters.

definitions.definition: When waves or states are in sync and work together in a predictable way.
definitions.example: Laser light is coherent because all the light waves are perfectly aligned.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Pre-Fall / The Fall

definitions.definition: The process where a quantum system loses its special quantum properties by interacting with its environment.
definitions.example: Like a spinning top that slowly wobbles and stops because of friction with the air.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Pre-Fall / The Fall

definitions.definition: The perspective or reference point from which you observe and measure something.
definitions.example: If you're in a moving car, your measurement frame is different from someone standing still.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Pre-Fall / The Fall

definitions.definition: The way a 3D object casts a 2D shadow or image onto a surface.
definitions.example: A globe's shadow on a wall is a projection of the Earth.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Pre-Fall / The Fall

definitions.definition: Broken into pieces, not just split in two.
definitions.example: A dropped mirror fractures into many shards.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Pre-Fall / The Fall

definitions.definition: The belief that God became a human being in the person of Jesus Christ.
definitions.example: Christmas celebrates the incarnation of God as a baby.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Constructive — Creation / Incarnation

definitions.definition: Coming back to life after being dead.
definitions.example: Jesus rising from the tomb on Easter Sunday.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Constructive — Creation / Incarnation

definitions.definition: Complete destruction, when matter and antimatter meet and turn into pure energy.
definitions.example: When a particle and its antiparticle collide, they annihilate in a flash of energy.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 2 > Destructive — Death / Decay

definitions.definition: A force that acts between electrically charged particles, including light and magnetism.
definitions.example: Magnets sticking to a fridge and radio waves are both electromagnetism.

definitions.definition: Travels or spreads through a medium or space.
definitions.example: Sound propagates through air; light propagates through a vacuum.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how waves, like sound or light, move.
definitions.example: The equation that predicts how ripples spread when you drop a stone in a pond.

definitions.definition: When two waves meet and cancel each other out, creating no wave at all.
definitions.example: Noise-canceling headphones use destructive interference to silence background noise.

definitions.definition: When a wave is flipped upside down so its peaks become valleys and vice versa.
definitions.example: If you take a sine wave and shift it by half a cycle, it's phase-inverted.

definitions.definition: The force that holds the nucleus of an atom together, the strongest known force.
definitions.example: It's what keeps protons and neutrons from flying apart inside an atom.

definitions.definition: A mathematical model that describes the strong force, including both attraction and confinement.
definitions.example: Like a rubber band that pulls harder the more you stretch it.

definitions.definition: The property that quarks inside a proton feel almost no force when very close together.
definitions.example: Like being in a crowded elevator where you can move freely if everyone is packed tight.

definitions.definition: A serious, binding promise or agreement, often between God and people.
definitions.example: Marriage is a covenant between two people.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Constructive — Love / Covenant

definitions.definition: The process that keeps quarks trapped inside particles like protons, never alone.
definitions.example: Like a force field that prevents you from ever leaving a room.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Destructive — Captivity / Addiction

definitions.definition: In a way that is harmful, unhealthy, or abnormal.
definitions.example: A cell growing pathologically is cancer.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Destructive — Captivity / Addiction

definitions.definition: When a force becomes too strong, causing a system to become stuck or trapped.
definitions.example: Glue that is so strong you can't separate two pieces of paper.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Destructive — Captivity / Addiction

definitions.definition: A bond so strong that it overflows to connect others, even at a cost to oneself.
definitions.example: A firefighter running into a burning building to save others shows sacrificial cohesion.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Free Will Equation

definitions.definition: The leftover strong force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
definitions.example: Like the leftover glue that sticks two pieces of paper together after the main glue dries.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Free Will Equation

definitions.definition: A finding that stable relationships need five positive interactions for every one negative.
definitions.example: For every criticism, you need five compliments to keep a relationship healthy.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 4 > Shannon Channel Capacity

definitions.definition: The branch of physics that deals with very small particles like atoms and electrons.
definitions.example: It explains why electrons can be in two places at once until you look at them.

definitions.definition: The ability of a quantum particle to be in multiple states at the same time until measured.
definitions.example: A coin spinning in the air is both heads and tails until it lands.

definitions.definition: When a quantum system's superposition suddenly becomes one definite state due to measurement.
definitions.example: The spinning coin landing on heads is a collapse from both possibilities to one.

definitions.definition: Cannot be undone or reversed.
definitions.example: Breaking an egg is irreversible; you can't put it back together.

definitions.definition: How fast a quantum system loses its special quantum properties and becomes normal.
definitions.example: How quickly a spinning top slows down and stops due to friction.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 5 > Destructive — Doubt / Decoherence

definitions.definition: The separate, ordinary realities that result from decoherence, each with definite outcomes.
definitions.example: In one branch you chose chocolate ice cream; in another, vanilla.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 5 > Destructive — Doubt / Decoherence

definitions.definition: The study of heat, energy, and how they move and change.
definitions.example: It explains why a hot cup of coffee cools down over time.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; it always increases over time.
definitions.example: Your room naturally gets messier over time unless you clean it—that's entropy.

definitions.definition: The law that says entropy always increases in a closed system; things tend toward disorder.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle because the water molecules become more disordered.

definitions.definition: The energy in a system that is available to do useful work.
definitions.example: The energy in a battery that can power a toy is free energy.

definitions.definition: Cruel and unfair rule or control by a person or group.
definitions.example: A king who punishes everyone for small mistakes is a tyrant.

definitions.definition: A result that involves changes in heat, energy, or disorder.
definitions.example: Running a marathon has the thermodynamic consequence of making you hot and sweaty.

definitions.definition: Adding energy from outside a system to change its behavior.
definitions.example: Plugging in a phone charger is an external energy injection.

definitions.definition: A possible end of the universe where everything is the same temperature and no work can be done.
definitions.example: Like a cup of coffee that has cooled to room temperature and can't get hot again.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 6 > Destructive — Judgment Without Mercy

definitions.definition: A state where everything is balanced and nothing changes.
definitions.example: A seesaw with two kids of equal weight is in equilibrium.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 6 > Destructive — Judgment Without Mercy

definitions.definition: Differences in something like temperature or pressure across a space.
definitions.example: A hot stove and a cold pan create a temperature gradient that cooks food.
definitions.first_appearance: Core Framework > Law 6 > Destructive — Judgment Without Mercy

definitions.definition: A force that causes certain types of radioactive decay and changes particle types.
definitions.example: It's responsible for the beta decay that makes a neutron turn into a proton.

definitions.definition: A type of radioactive decay where a neutron turns into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino.
definitions.example: A process that helps power the sun by changing particles.

definitions.definition: Changing one element into another, like turning lead into gold.
definitions.example: In stars, hydrogen is transmuted into helium through fusion.

definitions.definition: The process inside stars that creates heavier elements from lighter ones.
definitions.example: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium, then helium into carbon, and so on.

definitions.definition: Feeling sorry for wrongdoing and deciding to change your behavior.
definitions.example: Admitting you lied and promising to tell the truth from now on.
